title: graphictees
text: Published in 1920 by an emerging F. Scott Fitzgerald, “This Side of Paradise” follows Amory Blaine, a wealthy, narcissistic Midwesterner in a classic bildungsroman tale of losing worldly wealth and finding self-awareness, losing the means but finding the ends. While The Great Gatsby has overtaken Amory’s story as his seminal work, This Side of Paradise has a sicker (more sick?) claim to fame in my opinion - being the first to use the term “T-shirt” in print, as part of a packing list before Amory heads off to Princeton: “So early in September Amory, provided with ‘six suits summer underwear, six suits winter underwear, one sweater or T shirt, one jersey, one overcoat, winter, etc.,’ set out for New England, the land of schools.”

Of course, he didn’t invent the word; it had simply not been set down on a page before (that we know of). Like many other fashion trends and practices in the 20th century, World War II was behind the t-shirt’s - and eventually the graphic tee’s - emergence. Strangely, we (i.e., the internet as observed through my shitty, LLM-overview-attention-span-shortened web search abilities) seem to be uncertain how graphic tees came about. One theory is that factory workers in England cut the bottom half of their long johns off, creating the proto-t-shirt which natural-selectioned their way into popularity throughout the late 1800s. What we do know is that t-shirts became standard issue for US Army soldiers in training camps by the time the bad man (bad men?) started doing bad things on the other side of the Atlantic (and Pacific?).

As these homo sapiens soldiers grew to love their new t-shaped shirts, they began to customize these things they loved to communicate their allegiance and identity to others of their own species, as homo sapiens tend to do. They inked their insignias, units, home bases, and deployments onto their shirts using paint and stencils, a practice brought to mainstream America through Corporal Alexander Le Gerda’s appearance with his tight fitting t-shirt - “Air Corps / Las Vegas Nevada / Gunnery School” splayed across the front - on the cover of the July 13th, 1942 issue of LIFE Magazine. Soon, although it originated as a form of personal expression, throughout the 50s and 60s, America began to do the thing it tends to do with cultural products: optimize its mass manufacture. Screen printing in the 50s, Plastisol Ink in 1959, Andy-Warhol-style screen printing of photos in the 60s, the dual rotating printing press in 1969, and finally inkjet printing in 1996.

In my own (admittedly incomplete) bildungsroman tale, graphic tees joined the party early and never left. As I gained self-awareness in my early teenage/middle school years, I needed to acquire various hallmarks to prove to others and myself I was someone, and the 5 dollar graphic tees my mom grabbed to dress me for less (“KID OF THE YEAR”, in block lettering, from the clearance rack) metamorphosed into 30 dollar Hearthstone x UNIQLO t-shirts. I thought I was the shit for having this tee - for all of about a month, at which point Hearthstone became the card game for “dumbasses who spend money on a pay-to-win, virtual, game for losers”, as my friend from church who’d introduced me to Hearthstone put it. Safe to say that tee has not been further than 250 feet from my bedroom since.

Each new chapter of my life has brought a new “best tee of all time”: BHS BAO (Berkeley High School, Band and Orchestra, for the layperson), Firebird Suite edition in 9th grade, Team 5499 with its NASA (so cool) and Google (money is good?) sponsors in 10th grade, Cowell College in my first year of college, Stevenson College in my second. The latest: A 2002 AMD Athlon 64 launch day t-shirt, the first 64-bit processor targeted at the average consumer.

The 2023 Heddels article that I ripped the above history of graphic tees off of says this in its opening lines: “Fashion, in all its many forms, can be distilled down to the physical manifestation of our personalities. You could say that what we wear speaks to who we are without using words”. Those lines, in conversation with these lines below from Langdon Winner’s 1980 piece “Do artifacts have politics?”, nuance and enlarge our understanding of the space graphic tees have dug out within our society:

“None of the arguments and examples considered thus far addresses a stronger, more troubling claim often made in writings about technology and society—the belief that some technologies are by their very nature political in a specific way. According to this view, the adoption of a given technical system unavoidably brings with it conditions for human relationships that have a distinctive political cast—for example, centralized or decentralized, egalitarian or inegalitarian, repressive or liberating. This is ultimately what is at stake in assertions such as those of Lewis Mumford that two traditions of technology, one authoritarian, the other democratic, exist side by side in Western history… In this conception some kinds of technology require their social environments to be structured in a particular way in much the same sense that an automobile requires wheels in order to move. The thing could not exist as an effective operating entity unless certain social as well as material conditions were met.”

I’ll wear my favorite tee proudly, and it’ll always be the first one off the top of my t-shirt stack every wash cycle - until one day, it gently becomes the second off the top - and eventually, the last one, reserved for laundry day. But unlike in the past, these days, my t-shirt turnover rate seems not to be accelerated by off-hand comments by a friend, tilted from being OTK’d by Exodia Mage in Hearthstone, but by an almost imperceptible, glacial realization that my unique graphic-tee-based identity is ironically mass-manufactured, at which point I must pilgrimage to my local identity inheritance facility: the thrift store. What does this cycle say about me? Each Super Bowl, we make around 200,000 graphic tees that will be used when the final whistle is blown, and another 200,000 that proclaim loudly, passionately, with certainty, that the losing team won. What does it say about us, that donning championship identity as soon as humanly possible is worth more than 2 million dollars of excess?

Graphic tees speak to who we are, as a species, without using words: their graphic invention must be revolutionary, yet inherently they rely on being corporate for meaning. Liberating, and repressive. Decentralized, and centralized. This is humanity as we attempt to make sense of how to live with one another.
All this being said, I hope Amory packs a blank white t-shirt. They go with more outfits, in my experience.
I give graphic tees 4.5 stars out of 5.
